  Process for Annual Assessment
In each subsequent year for which the assessment will be continued and as required by the procedures
specified in the 1972 Act, an Engineer’s Report must be prepared on an annual basis which contains a full
and detailed description of the improvements, the boundaries of the assessment district and any zones
therein, and the proposed assessments upon assessable lots and parcels of land within the assessment
district.
The City Council must also annually adopt a resolution of intention which:

    Declares the intention of the City Council to levy and collect assessments within the assessment
  district for the fiscal year stated therein.

    Generally describes the existing and proposed improvements and any substantial changes
  proposed to be made in existing improvements.
    Refers to the assessment district by its distinctive designation and indicates the general location of
  the assessment district.

    Refers to the report of the engineer, on file with the City Clerk, for a full and detailed description of
  the improvements, the boundaries of the assessment district and any zones therein, and the
  proposed assessments upon assessable lots and parcels of land within the assessment district.

    Gives notice of the time and place for public hearing by the City Council on the levy of the
  proposed assessment.

    States whether the assessment is proposed to increase from the previous year.
If the assessments are to be levied in the same or lesser amounts than the maximum assessment allowed,
the City Clerk shall give notice of the public hearing by causing the resolution of intention to be published.
Any interested person may, prior to the conclusion of the public hearing, file a written protest which shall
state all grounds of objection. The protest shall contain a description sufficient to identify the property
owned by the property owner filing the protest. During the course or upon conclusion of the hearing, the
City Council may order changes in any of the matters provided in the report, including changes in the
improvements, any zones within the assessment district, and the proposed diagram or the proposed
assessment. If the assessment to be levied exceeds the maximum assessment allowed, the City must
comply with the procedures specified in Article XIII D and Proposition 218.
The City Council, upon conclusion of the public hearing must then adopt a resolution confirming the
diagram and assessment, either as originally proposed or as changed by it. The adoption of the resolution
shall constitute the levy of an assessment for the fiscal year referred to in the assessment. If confirmed, the
assessments would be submitted to the County Auditor Controller for inclusion on the property tax roll.

   Legislative Context
In 1996, California Voters adopted Proposition 218, the “Right to Vote on Taxes Act” which added Articles
XIII C and XIII D to the California Constitution. Article XIII D imposes certain substantive and procedural
requirements on any agency that wishes to levy special assessments.
Article XIII D imposes four basic substantive requirements on assessments1:

    All parcels that will have a special benefit conferred upon them and upon which an assessment will
  be imposed must be identified;
    The general benefits must be distinguished from the special benefits conferred on the parcels;

    The proportionate special benefit derived by each parcel must be determined in relationship to the
  entirety of the capital improvement, the maintenance and operation expenses of the public
  improvement, or the cost of the property related service being provided; and

    The amount assessed to a parcel must not exceed the reasonable cost of the proportional special
  benefit conferred on that parcel and does not include any costs attributable to the general benefit.
Since the initial passage of Proposition 218, several court rulings have helped provide context and direction
on the practical implementation procedures and requirements for levying assessments. Several of the key
concepts from these rulings are summarized below.
GENERAL BENEFIT
Article XIII D requires an agency to separate the general benefits from the special benefits conferred
because only special benefits are assessable.
The Court of Appeal in Golden Hills Neighborhood Assn., Inc. v. City of San Diego (2011) (Golden Hills)2
clarified this concept by stating, “Separation and quantification of general and special benefits must be
accomplished by apportioning the cost of a service or improvement between the two and assessing
property owners only for the portion of the cost representing special benefits.”
The Court of Appeal in Beutz v. County of Riverside (2010) (Beutz)3 quoted from the Legislative Analyst’s
Office pamphlet titled “Understanding Proposition 218” which states an agency must, “estimate the
amount of special benefit landowners would receive from the project or service, as well as the amount of
‘general benefit.’ This step is needed because Proposition 218 allows local government to recoup from
assessments only the proportionate share of cost to provide the special benefit.”
The Court in Beutz furthered this idea stating, “Separating the general from the special benefits of a public
improvement project and estimating the quantity of each in relation to the other is essential if an
assessment is to be limited to the special benefits.”
The Court of Appeal in Silicon Valley Taxpayers' Association Incorporated v. Santa Clara County Open Space
Authority (2008) (SVTA) 4 clarified that general benefits are not restricted to benefits conferred only on
persons and property outside the assessment district but can include benefits both conferred on real

 property located in the district or to the public at large. The “public at large” includes all members of the
public, including those who live, work, and shop within the district, and not simply transient visitors.
BENEFIT-BASED NOT COST-BASED
In Bonander v. Town of Tiburon (2009) (Tiburon)5, the Court of Appeal clarified the idea that assessments
must be apportioned based upon benefit rather than cost. The Court stated, “Proportionate special benefit
is the basis upon which a project’s total assessable costs are apportioned among parcels within an
assessment district.”
The assessment on a particular property cannot be based on the relative cost of the improvements, but
rather the special benefit conferred on such property. The Court in Tiburon also stated, “an assessment
represents the entirety of the cost of the improvement or property-related service, less any amount
attributable to general benefits (which may not be assessed), allocated to individual properties in
proportion to the relative special benefit conferred on the property.”
PUBLIC PROPERTY
Section 4, Subdivision (a) of Article XIII D states, in part, “Parcels within a district that are owned or used by
any agency, the State of California or the United States shall not be exempt from assessment unless the
agency can demonstrate by clear and convincing evidence that those publicly owned parcels in fact receive
no special benefit.” Historically there had been differing opinions about whether this requirement that
publicly owned property should not be exempt actually meant those properties must be assessed.
The Court of Appeal in Manteca Unified School District v. Reclamation District No. 17 et al (2017)
(Manteca)6 clarified this issue by stating, “section 4, subdivision (a) of article XIII D of the California
Constitution unambiguously conditions any continuing benefit assessment exemption on a showing by clear
and convincing evidence of no special benefit.”
IMPRECISION
The Court in Tiburon acknowledged the difficulty of trying to precisely assign and measure special benefit,
stating, “Any attempt to classify special benefits conferred on particular properties and to assign relative
weights to those benefits will necessarily involve some degree of imprecision.”
The Court in Tiburon went on to say that a formula assigning equal weight to different special benefits
“may be a legally justifiable approach to measuring and apportioning special benefits, [but] it is not
necessarily the only valid approach. Whichever approach is taken to measuring and apportioning special
benefits, however, it must be both defensible and consistently applied.”

   METHOD OF APPORTIONMENT
The following section includes an explanation of the benefits to be derived from the installation,
maintenance and servicing of the improvements throughout each District, as well as a description of the
assessment methodology used to apportion the total assessment to properties within each District.
Previous annual Engineer’s Reports were prepared by a different engineer of record and language from
the prior year Engineer’s Report9 has been referenced to describe the Method of Apportionment within
the following section of this report.10
The Districts consist of all assessor parcels within the boundaries as defined by the Assessment Diagram
included with this report and the parcels identified by the Assessor Parcel Numbers listed with the
included levy roll. The parcel list includes all privately and publicly owned parcels with the boundaries. The
method used for apportioning the assessment is based on the proportional special benefits to be derived
by the properties in the Districts over and above general benefits conferred on real property or to the
public at large. The apportionment of special benefit is a two-step process: the first step is to identify the
types of special benefit arising from the improvements, and the second step is to allocate the assessments
to property based on the estimated relative special benefit for each type of property.

  General Versus Special Benefit
General benefit is an overall and similar benefit to the public at large resulting from the improvements to
be maintained by the assessments levied. Specific language describing the relationship and proportion of
Special Benefit versus General Benefit from the Prior Engineer’s Report has been included below:
The proceeds from the Districts are used to fund increased levels of maintenance to the Districts’
improvements that serve and benefit the properties in the Districts. In the absence of the Districts, such
improvements would not be properly maintained. Therefore, the Districts’ purpose is to ensure that the
necessary and beneficial public facilities for property in the Districts are properly maintained and repaired
over time. The assessments will ensure that street lighting and associated improvements within and
adjacent to the Districts are functional, well maintained and safe. These public resources directly benefit
the property in the Districts and will confer distinct and special benefits to the properties within the
Districts. Moreover, the absence of the improvements, a condition of development would not be met and
future construction in the Districts could be denied. The creation of individual lots, if any, and the
approval for construction in the Districts, is the overriding clear and distinct special benefit conferred
exclusively on property in the Districts and not enjoyed by other properties outside the Districts.
Therefore, the improvements provide special benefit to property in the Districts over and above the
general benefits conferred to the public at large or properties outside the Districts.
Although the improvements maintained by the services may be available to the general public at large,
the improvements and services are specifically designed, located and created to provide additional and
improved resources for property inside the Districts, and not the public at large. Other properties that are
outside the Districts do not enjoy the unique proximity and other special benefit factors described

Districts because they provide a direct advantage to properties in the Districts that would not be provided
in the absence of the improvements. Any general benefits to surrounding properties outside of the

   Cost of Living Inflator
Annually, the amount of assessments for the Districts may be increased, based upon the Consumer Price
Index, All Urban Consumers, for Los Angeles-Long Beach-Anaheim Area ("CPI"), as determined by the
United States Department of Labor, Bureau of Labor Statistics, or its successor. The Assessment Engineer
shall compute the percentage difference between the CPI for February of the current year and the CPI for
the previous February, and shall then adjust the existing assessment by an amount not to exceed such
percentage for the following fiscal year. Should the Bureau of Labor Statistics revise such index or
discontinue the preparation of such index, the Assessment Engineer shall use the revised index or a
comparable system as approved by the City Council for determining fluctuations in the cost of living.
Alternatively, Assessment Districts Nos. 1, 2, 3, and 4 may use the Southern California Edison and
California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) approved rates for each light fixture adjustment schedule as
the basis for adjustment of the annual rates. As a result, the assessment may be continued to be levied
annually and may be increased by up to the maximum annual CPI adjustment (or CPUC adjustment for
Assessment Districts Nos. 1, 2, 3, and 4), without any additional assessment ballot proceeding. Further, in
the event that in future years the assessments are levied at a rate less than the maximum authorized
assessment rate, the assessment rate in a subsequent year may be increased up to the maximum
authorized assessment rate without any additional assessment ballot proceeding. 13
For Fiscal Year 2021/22, the maximum authorized assessment rates for the Districts are increased by
0.97%, based on the increase of the February 2020 to February 2021 CPI, for All Urban Consumers in the
Los Angeles-Long Beach- Anaheim Area, of 0.97%.

  Fiscal Year 2021/22 Maximum Assessment
The Fiscal Year 2021/22 maximum authorized assessment rates for the Districts are included in Section 8
of this Engineer’s Report.

  Duration of Assessment
The Districts were formed or annexed in previous years. It is proposed that the assessments be continued
every year after their formation or annexation, so long as the public improvements need to be maintained
and improved, and the City requires funding from the assessments for these improvements in each
District. As noted previously, the assessment can continue to be levied annually after the City Council
approves an annually updated Engineer’s Report, budget for the assessment, improvements to be
provided, and other specifics of the assessment. In addition, the City Council must hold an annual public
hearing to continue the assessment.

  Appeals and Interpretation
Any property owner who feels that the assessment levied on the subject property is in error, as a result of
incorrect information being used to apply the foregoing method of assessment, may file a written appeal
with the City of Palmdale Public Works department. Any such appeal is limited to correction of an
assessment during the then current fiscal year or, if before July 1, the upcoming fiscal year. Upon the filing

SUBJECT:  ADOPT RESOLUTION NO. CC 2021-043, A RESOLUTION OF THE
  CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF PALMDALE UPDATING THE
  SEWER COLLECTION SERVICE CHARGE AND ORDERING THE
  CONTINUATION OF THE CHARGE FOR THE OPERATION AND
  MAINTENANCE OF THE PALMDALE SEWER COLLECTION
  SYSTEM FOR FISCAL YEAR 2021/2022
ISSUE
Hold a public hearing to accept public testimony and adopt Resolution No. CC 2021-
043, relative to updating the Sewer Collection Service Charge and ordering the
continuation of the charge for the operation and maintenance of the Palmdale sewer
collection system.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council accept public testimony and adopt Resolution
No. CC 2021-043.

BACKGROUND
In July 2009, the City took over maintenance and operation of the sewer collection
system from the Consolidated Sewer Maintenance District (CSMD) of Los Angeles
County. At that time, the City withdrew from CSMD and became responsible for the
maintenance, operation, repair, rehabilitation, and replacement of the sewer collection
system within the City boundary. The City-owned collection facilities convey wastewater
to trunk sewers and treatment facilities owned by Sanitation Districts #14 and #20 of Los
Angeles County.

In order to fund the operation and maintenance of the sewer collection system, the City
initiated notification and protest proceedings as specified in Section 53750 of the
California State Government Code and Article XIII D of the California State Constitution.
On June 18, 2008, the City Council held the public hearing. A majority of property owners
did not present written protests, and therefore the City Council passed Resolution CC
2008-056 which adopted the Fee. Additionally, on June 18, 2008, the City Council
adopted Ordinance 1353 adopting Chapter 13.05 of the Palmdale Municipal Code
establishing a Sewer Collection Service Charge. On April 1, 2009, the City Council
 Report to Mayor and City Council

adopted Ordinance 1361 amending Section 13.05.130 of Chapter 13.05 of the Palmdale
Municipal Code clarifying the service rates for government and school properties.

In 2020, the City initiated a rate study to review the sewer collection service charges.
The “Sewer Service Charge Analysis, Five Year Rate Proposal” (the “Rate Study”) was
completed by Bartle Wells Associates in April 2020. The Rate Study determined that the
City currently receives sufficient revenues from the Fee to provide its sewer collection
services, sewer related repairs, and capital projects. The analysis further states that the
sewer enterprise is in good financial condition, and the Fee should continue to be
applied unchanged at the rate of $103.63 per sewage unit for five years, from Fiscal
Year 2020/21 to Fiscal Year 2024/25.

The City Council will consider today adoption of Resolution No. CC 2021-043, which
orders the continuation of the levy of the Fee for Fiscal Year 2021/2022.

DISCUSSION
The City has worked with NBS to prepare the Fiscal Year 2021/2022 Sewer Collection
Service Charge Report dated June 2021, which contains the methodology for determining
the Fee and assigning it to each parcel, estimates the cost for operations and
maintenance of the sewer collection system, and lists the rate of the Fee.

The City Council will hold a public hearing regarding the approval of the Fiscal Year
2021/2022 Sewer Collection Service Charge Report dated June 2021 and the ordering of
the levy for Fiscal Year 2021/2022. Following the public hearing, the City Council will
consider adoption of Resolution No. CC 2021-043, ordering the continuation of the charge
for the operation and maintenance of the City’s sewer collection system and the
continuation of the levy and collection of the Fee on the Los Angeles County tax rolls.

FISCAL IMPACT
Details of the Fee are within the Fiscal Year 2021/2022 Sewer Collection Service
Charge Report, dated June 2021, included as an attachment.

Approval of the Fee would result in revenues that would fund the maintenance and
operation of the sewer collection system owned by the City for Fiscal Year 2021/2022.
The Fee for Fiscal Year 2021/2022 is $103.63 per sewage unit, which is the same rate
since Fiscal Year 2010/2011. The proposed total Fee for Fiscal Year 2021/2022 is
$5,470,627.51.

 1. INTRODUCTION
  Background
In July 2009, the City of Palmdale (the “City”) took over the maintenance and operation of the sewer
collection system from the Consolidated Sewer Maintenance District (CSMD) of Los Angeles County. At
that time, the City withdrew from the CSMD and became responsible for the maintenance, operation,
repair, rehabilitation, and replacement of the sewer collection system within the City’s boundary. The City-
owned collection facilities convey wastewater to trunk sewers and treatment facilities owned by Sanitation
Districts #14 and #20 of Los Angeles County.
In order to fund the operation and maintenance of the sewer collection system, the City initiated
notification and protest proceedings as specified in Section 53750 of the California State Government Code
and Article XIII D of the California State Constitution. Notices were mailed to property owners in areas
currently served by the municipal sewer system or likely to be served by the municipal sewer system in the
future. The notice explained the reason for the proposed Sewer Collection Service Charge (the “Fee”), the
method by which the Fee is calculated, and the rates for Fiscal Years 2008/09, 2009/10, and 2010/11. The
notice also included the time, date, and place of a public hearing for the Fee, and instructions that property
owners could file written protests against implementation of the Fee. The notice specified that if a majority
of property owners filed written protests, the Fee would not be charged.
On June 18, 2008, the City held the public hearing. A majority of property owners did not present written
protests, and therefore the City passed Resolution CC 2008-082 which adopted the Fee.
In 2020, the City ordered a rate study to evaluate the sewer collection service charges for the next five
fiscal years. The “Sewer Service Charge Analysis, Five Year Rate Proposal” (the “Rate Study”) was
completed by Bartle Wells Associates in April 2020. The Rate Study shows that the City currently receives
enough revenues from the Fee to provide its sewer collection services, sewer related repairs, and capital
projects. The Rate Study analysis further states that the sewer enterprise is in good financial condition, and
an increased rate above the current rate of $103.63 per sewage unit is not anticipated for five years.
The Fee funds only the maintenance and operation of the sewer collection system within the City and does
not fund the maintenance and operation of either the trunk sewers or wastewater treatment facilities.

  Process for Annual Fee
The resolution adopting the Fee specified that a written report shall be filed annually with the City Clerk,
which contains a description of each parcel of real property receiving the Fee and the amount of the
charge for each parcel for the year, computed as described by the resolution.
The City Clerk shall give notice of the filing of the written report, and of the time and place of the public
hearing thereon. The City Council shall hear and consider all objections or protests, if any. Upon conclusion
of the hearing, the City Council may adopt, revise, change, reduce or modify any charge or overrule any or
all objections and shall make its determination upon each charge as described in said report.

  City of Palmdale
  Sewer Collection Service Charge - Fiscal Year 2021/22 Sewer Fee Report  1
 The Fee is collected at the same time and in the same manner as County taxes. The Fee roll is submitted
each year to the Los Angeles County Auditor in August for inclusion on the Los Angeles County property tax
bill.

  Legislative Context
In 1996, California Voters adopted Proposition 218, the “Right to Vote on Taxes Act” which added Articles
XIII C and XIII D to the California Constitution. Article XIII D, Section 6, specifically describes property
related fees.
Proposition 218 provides for property-related fees to be levied to fund the cost of providing services,
including sewer service, to property. Proposition 218 describes a number of important requirements,
including property-owner notification and public hearings, for the imposition, increase, and extension of
fees, and these requirements are satisfied by the process used to establish this Fee.

 3. ESTIMATE OF COSTS
Revenue from the collection of the Fee will fund expenses incurred by the City related to the operation and
maintenance of its sewer collection system. These expenses include costs for labor, engineering and
support staff time, staff and operating facilities, materials, equipment, operation, and maintenance of the
sewer collection system. The City must also generate revenue to perform repairs, rehabilitation, and
replacement of aging sewer mains. Capital expenditures are included in the estimated costs.
An initial five-year estimate of expenses required to operate and maintain the City sewer collection system
was developed by City staff. These expenses include salaries and benefits for City staff that will be
performing the maintenance and operational activities, professional engineering consulting services, and
equipment purchases.
As previously mentioned, Bartle Wells Associates prepared a Rate Study in April 2020 to review the City
revenues and expenses, in order to evaluate if the current Fee rate of $103.63 per sewage unit is adequate
or if it should be increased. The Rate Study shows that the City currently receives enough funding from the
annual Fee to provide its operation and maintenance of the sewer collection system, and to perform sewer
related repairs and expansion as needed. It was also anticipated that the current sewage unit charge of
$103.63 will be sufficient for the following five years. Therefore, the City plans on continuing assessing the
same charge of $103.63 per sewage unit for the five years, from Fiscal Year 2020/21 through 2024/25.

 4. METHOD AND RATE OF CALCULATION
Determination of the Fee for each parcel served by the City sewer system is a two-part process:

  •  First, each parcel is assigned the appropriate number of sewage units based on the property type
  and land use of the parcel. The sewage units are listed in Table 2. Sewage Units by Property Type
  and correspond to the quantity of wastewater that a parcel discharges to the sewer collection
  system. One sewage unit is a benchmark value representing the quantity of wastewater discharged
  by a typical single-family residence. Since the Fee funds the maintenance and operation of the
  sewer collection system, the quantity of wastewater is of primary interest while the quality of
  wastewater has little or no effect on system operation. Therefore, the Fee is apportioned based on
  the quantity of wastewater conveyed from a parcel.

  •  The next step is to determine the total revenue required and the number of sewage units for
  parcels served by the City’s sewer collection system. The total revenue required is $5,470,627.51
  as shown in Table 5. Budget Allocation to Property for Fiscal Year 2021/22. There are currently
  52,790 sewage units within the area served by the City sewer collection system. Therefore, the Fee
  for Fiscal Year 2021/22 is $103.63 per sewage unit.
This rate of $103.63 per sewage unit remains unchanged and is the same rate used since Fiscal Year
2010/11, as it was specified in the notice mailed to property owners in 2008, as well as the April 2008
Engineer’s Report referenced in Resolution No. CC 2008-082 of the Palmdale City Council, dated June 18,
2008. Furthermore, the rate per sewage unit is also supported by the Bartle Wells Associates Rate Study
dated April 2020.
This Fee represents the proportional cost of service attributable to each parcel as specified in Article XIII D,
Section 6(b)(3) of the California State Constitution which specifies that:
  The amount of a fee or charge imposed upon any parcel or person as an incident of property
  ownership shall not exceed the proportional cost of the service attributable to the parcel.
Fees for sewer collection are “property-related fees and charges” as described in Article XIII D of the
California State Constitution.

BACKGROUND
On September 10, 2020, the City of Palmdale Planning Commission approved
Conditional Use Permit (CUP) 19-007 for a proposed banquet facility (Palmdale Event
Hall). The banquet hall currently holds a Type 58 Department of Alcoholic Beverage

ISSUE
Shall the City Council adopt Resolution No. CC 2021-067 Amending the City’s
Classification and Pay Plan for General Positions?

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council adopt Resolution No. CC 2021-067 Amending
the City’s Classification and Pay Plan for General Positions.

BACKGROUND
The Human Resources Division monitors and evaluates positions within the organization
and makes recommendations based on the needs of the City.

DISCUSSION
At the June 15, 2021 City Council meeting, the Fiscal Year 2021-22 budget was approved.
As a result, the City’s Classification and Pay Plan for General Positions has been updated
and requires City Council approval.

The following positions within the City’s management team received the same 5%
increase as the other full-time positions listed in the Classification and Pay Plan for
General Employees: Assistant City Manager, Director of Public Works, Deputy City
Manager, Director of Economic & Community Development, Director of Neighborhood
Services, and Director of Parks & Recreation.

The City Manager and City Attorney each received a 2% increase.

In addition, the California Public Employees’ Retirement System (CalPERS) requires the
City to approve Classification and Pay Plans separately, not in combination with other
items on the agenda, such as the budget. To comply with CalPERS guidelines, staff is
submitting the Classification and Pay Plan for General Positions for approval.
